norse_hodr.name: slays the invulnerable Baldr with the mistletoe dart
norse_hodr.notes: Gylfaginning: blind Hǫðr, guided by Loki, throws the one thing that can harm Baldr — the mistletoe — and kills his brother.

sources.reference: Snorri Sturluson, Gylfaginning (Prose Edda), ch. 49; Vǫluspá 31-32 (Poetic Edda)

norse_idunn.name: keeps and dispenses the apples that hold off the gods' old age
norse_idunn.notes: Snorri's Skáldskaparmál names her keeper of the apples the Æsir bite to ward off old age until Ragnarök; her loss to Þjazi causes the gods to wither.

sources.reference: Snorri Sturluson, Skáldskaparmál (Prose Edda), ch. on Iðunn

norse_idunn.name: restores the youth of the aging gods
norse_idunn.notes: The apples she guards renew the Æsir's youth; without her the gods grow grey and old (Haustlöng; Skáldskaparmál).

norse_jord.name: is the personified Earth, the ground itself
norse_jord.notes: Snorri's Gylfaginning and Skáldskaparmál treat Jǫrð as the Earth personified, daughter of Nótt, mother of Thor by Odin; she is the land and soil.

sources.reference: Snorri Sturluson, Gylfaginning and Skáldskaparmál (Prose Edda)

norse_jord.name: bears Thor, the defender of the worlds, to Odin
norse_jord.notes: Thor is repeatedly called Jarðar burr ('son of Jǫrð'); she is among the foremost ancestresses of the Æsir.

norse_nanna.name: dies of grief at Baldr's death and follows him onto the pyre
norse_nanna.notes: Gylfaginning: when Baldr is laid on Hringhorni, Nanna's heart breaks with grief and she dies and is burned beside him.

norse_nanna.name: sends gifts back from Hel to Frigg and Fulla
norse_nanna.notes: From Hel she gives Hermóðr a linen robe for Frigg and a finger-ring for Fulla to carry back to the living.

norse_rindr.name: bears Váli, the avenger of Baldr, to Odin
norse_rindr.notes: Baldrs draumar foretells that Rindr will bear Váli in the western halls; the child avenges Baldr at one night old. Saxo (Gesta Danorum 3) tells how Othinus won Rinda by guile.

sources.reference: Baldrs draumar (Poetic Edda); Snorri, Gylfaginning; Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum bk. 3

norse_ran.name: gathers the drowned to her undersea hall
norse_ran.notes: Those lost at sea are said to 'go to Rán'; the wife of Ægir nets the drowned and receives them in her hall (Skáldskaparmál; Sonatorrek).

sources.reference: Snorri Sturluson, Skáldskaparmál (Prose Edda); Egill Skallagrímsson, Sonatorrek

norse_ymir.name: his slain body becomes the substance of the world
norse_ymir.notes: From Ymir's flesh the earth was made, from his blood the sea, from his bones the mountains, from his skull the heavens, from his brains the clouds (Grímnismál; Vafþrúðnismál; Gylfaginning).

sources.reference: Grímnismál 40-41 and Vafþrúðnismál 21 (Poetic Edda); Snorri, Gylfaginning

norse_ymir.name: engenders the race of frost-giants from his own body
norse_ymir.notes: As he slept, a man and woman grew from under his arm and his feet begot a son; thus the hrímþursar descend from Ymir.

norse_thjazi.name: takes the shape of a great eagle
norse_thjazi.notes: In eagle-form Þjazi forces Loki to deliver Iðunn and seizes her with her apples (Haustlöng; Skáldskaparmál).

sources.reference: Þjóðólfr of Hvinir, Haustlöng; Snorri, Skáldskaparmál

norse_thjazi.name: abducts Iðunn and her apples, withering the gods
norse_thjazi.notes: His theft of Iðunn ages the Æsir until Loki recovers her; pursuing, Þjazi is burned and killed at Asgard's walls.

norse_magni.name: possesses prodigious strength even as an infant
norse_magni.notes: At three nights old Magni alone lifts the giant Hrungnir's leg off the fallen Thor, when no other god could move it (Skáldskaparmál).

sources.reference: Snorri Sturluson, Skáldskaparmál (Prose Edda), the Hrungnir episode

norse_magni.name: inherits Mjǫllnir and survives Ragnarök with his brother
norse_magni.notes: Vafþrúðnismál: Móði and Magni shall possess Mjǫllnir when Vingnir (Thor) falls in the renewed world.

norse_modi.name: embodies battle-courage and wrath (his name means 'Courage/Wrath')
norse_modi.notes: Móði ('the angry/courageous one') is named among Thor's sons; the name itself denotes martial fury.

sources.reference: Snorri Sturluson, Skáldskaparmál (Prose Edda), kennings for Thor

norse_modi.name: inherits Mjǫllnir and survives Ragnarök with Magni
norse_modi.notes: Vafþrúðnismál foretells that Móði and Magni will wield their father's hammer in the world after Ragnarök.

norse_vali.name: grows to manhood in a single day to avenge Baldr
norse_vali.notes: Vǫluspá and Baldrs draumar: Váli, son of Odin and Rindr, neither washes his hands nor combs his hair until he has brought Baldr's slayer to the pyre, at one night old.

sources.reference: Vǫluspá 32-33 and Baldrs draumar (Poetic Edda); Snorri, Gylfaginning

norse_ve.name: with Odin and Vili slays Ymir and shapes the world
norse_ve.notes: Gylfaginning: the three sons of Borr — Odin, Vili and Vé — kill Ymir and fashion the cosmos from his body.

norse_ve.name: helps give the first humans countenance, speech and the senses
norse_ve.notes: Snorri's Gylfaginning assigns to the three brothers the gifts of breath, wit, and face/speech/hearing/sight to Askr and Embla.

norse_vili.name: with Odin and Vé slays Ymir and shapes the world
norse_vili.notes: One of the three sons of Borr who kill the frost-giant Ymir and build the world from his body (Gylfaginning).

norse_vili.name: helps give the first humans wit and motion (his name means 'Will')
norse_vili.notes: Vili ('will') is named with Vé as co-creator; the brothers endow Askr and Embla with the inner faculties.

sources.reference: Snorri Sturluson, Gylfaginning (Prose Edda), ch. 9; Lokasenna 26 (Poetic Edda)

norse_sigi.name: founds the Vǫlsung dynasty with Odin's favour
norse_sigi.notes: Half-divine son of Odin who, after slaying the thrall Breði and being banished, builds a kingdom with the god's help and begets the Vǫlsung line (Vǫlsunga saga ch. 1).

norse_sigmund.name: alone can draw Odin's sword Gram from the tree Barnstokkr
norse_sigmund.notes: At his sister Signý's wedding a one-eyed stranger (Odin) thrusts a sword into Barnstokkr; only Sigmund can pull it free (Vǫlsunga saga ch. 3).

norse_sinfjotli.name: gains the strength and howl of a wolf in the cursed wolf-skins
norse_sinfjotli.notes: With Sigmund he wears the enchanted wolf-pelts and lives as a beast in the forest, killing many men before the skins are burned (Vǫlsunga saga ch. 8).

norse_sigrun.name: as a valkyrie rides air and sea and shields her chosen warrior in battle
norse_sigrun.notes: Helgakviða Hundingsbana: Sigrún and her valkyrie company ride over sky and sea to ward Helgi in the fight against Hǫðbroddr.

norse_sigrun.name: chooses Helgi as her husband against her father's betrothal
norse_sigrun.notes: Refusing the match to Hǫðbroddr, she seeks out Helgi Hundingsbani and weds him after he wins the battle of Frekastein.

norse_signy.name: engineers the destruction of Siggeir across years of patient revenge
norse_signy.notes: Vǫlsunga saga: Signý tests her sons, conceives Sinfjǫtli by her own brother Sigmund to breed an avenger of pure Vǫlsung blood, then dies in the burning of Siggeir's hall she helped contrive.

norse_signy.name: exchanges her shape with a sorceress to lie unrecognised with Sigmund
norse_signy.notes: By witchcraft she takes another woman's form to come unknown to her brother and beget Sinfjǫtli.

norse_volsung.name: is conceived by the fertility-apple Frigg sends to Rerir
norse_volsung.notes: Vǫlsunga saga: Rerir's queen eats the apple sent by Óðinn's messenger from Frigg and bears Vǫlsung after a long pregnancy; he is cut living from his dying mother.

norse_jormunrekkr.name: has Svanhild trampled by horses and Randvér hanged on a slander
norse_jormunrekkr.notes: Believing the charge that his wife Svanhild and his son Randvér betrayed him, Jǫrmunrekkr hangs Randvér and has Svanhild trodden to death by horses (Hamðismál; Vǫlsunga saga).

sources.reference: Hamðismál (Poetic Edda); Vǫlsunga saga ch. 42; Snorri, Skáldskaparmál

norse_ragnar.name: slays Þóra's serpent in pitch-boiled breeches to win her hand
norse_ragnar.notes: Ragnar kills the great serpent coiled round the maiden Þóra's bower, warded from its venom by his shaggy pitch-soaked breeches, and so wins both bride and byname (Ragnars saga).

nuer_buk.name: is the mother of the rain-spirit Deng among the spirits of the above
nuer_buk.notes: Evans-Pritchard records Buk (Candit/Garang's consort in some accounts) as a female Spirit of the above, mother of Deng, associated with rivers and streams.

nuer_buk.name: dwells in and gives power over rivers and streams
nuer_buk.notes: Buk is the colwic/sky-spirit most closely linked with rivers; offerings to her are connected with the waters.

nuer_deng.name: sends the rain as the foremost spirit of the above
nuer_deng.notes: Deng, son of Buk, is the great Nuer (and Dinka) spirit of the sky and rain, invoked by prophets who 'carry Deng'.

sources.reference: E. E. Evans-Pritchard, Nuer Religion (1956); cf. Lienhardt, Divinity and Experience (Dinka Deng)

nuer_deng.name: brings fever and sickness on those he seizes
nuer_deng.notes: Deng is associated with epidemic sickness and fever; people fall ill when 'caught' by him, and sacrifice is made to release them.

nupe_gunnu.name: renews the fertility of the land through the annual Gunnu festival
nupe_gunnu.notes: Nadel documents the Gunnu as a fertility cult whose dry-season festival, with a boys' bush initiation, asks renewed fertility of the land and community.

sources.reference: S. F. Nadel, 'Gunnu, a Fertility Cult of the Nupe in Northern Nigeria' (JRAI, 1937); Nadel, Nupe Religion (1954)

nupe_kuti.name: wards the community against witchcraft as a tutelary cult-power
nupe_kuti.notes: The kuti power, embodied in the Ndakó Gboyá masquerade, polices and destroys witches; the masked 'tall grandfather' is 'the policeman of the Gunnu'.

sources.reference: S. F. Nadel, Nupe Religion (1954); Nadel, 'Witchcraft and Anti-Witchcraft in Nupe Society' (Africa, 1935)

norse_idunn.name: the ash-wood casket (eski) holding the apples of youth

sources.reference: Snorri Sturluson, Skáldskaparmál (Prose Edda), ch. on Iðunn-kennings

norse_jormungandr.name: world-poisoning venom that fills air and sea at Ragnarök

norse_nanna.name: the linen robe and finger-ring she sends from Hel to Frigg and Fulla

norse_surtr.name: the flaming sword brighter than the sun

sources.reference: Vǫluspá 52 (Poetic Edda); Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 4 and 51

norse_magni.name: Gullfaxi ('Golden-mane'), the horse of Hrungnir given him by Thor

sources.reference: Snorri Sturluson, Skáldskaparmál (Prose Edda), the Hrungnir episode

norse_sigi.name: the kingdom and warband Odin grants him to found the Vǫlsung line

norse_sinfjotli.name: the cursed wolf-skins he and Sigmund don to live as wolves

norse_sigrun.name: the valkyrie's helm and blood-reddened byrnie she wears riding the air

norse_ragnar.name: the shaggy hair-breeches (loðbrók) boiled in pitch that turn the serpent's venom

norse_sorli.name: the byrnie of the Jónakrssynir that iron could not bite

nupe_edegi.name: Egba Tsoede, the heavy magical iron chains that became the emblem of royal judicial power

sources.reference: S. F. Nadel, A Black Byzantium (1942)

nupe_edegi.name: the bronze canoe and the long brass trumpets (kakati) given him by the Igala king

sources.reference: S. F. Nadel, A Black Byzantium (1942)

nupe_kuti.name: the towering cloth Ndakó Gboyá masquerade ('the tall grandfather') wrapped like a shroud

norse_idunn.gloss: 'keeper of the apples' (the Æsir's age-old cure)

sources.reference: Snorri Sturluson, Skáldskaparmál (Prose Edda), ch. on Iðunn

norse_jord.gloss: the Earth (a poetic name of Jǫrð, mother of Thor)

sources.reference: Ragnars saga loðbrókar; Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum bk. 9
Fáfnismál (Poetic Edda); Vǫlsunga saga; Snorri, Skáldskaparmál

norse_ymir.gloss: a name of the primordial giant among the frost-giants

nuer_kwoth.gloss: 'Spirit who is in the sky / God in the heavens'

nupe_edegi.gloss: 'King of the Nupe', the royal title he founded

sources.reference: S. F. Nadel, A Black Byzantium (1942)
Þjóðólfr of Hvinir, Haustlöng; Snorri, Skáldskaparmál
Snorri Sturluson, Gylfaginning and Skáldskaparmál (Prose Edda)

norse_njord.name: the toast to Njǫrðr and Freyr for plenty and peace at the sacrificial feast

term.value: Njarðar full ok Freys full til árs ok friðar
term.rom: Njarðar full ok Freys full til árs ok friðar

norse_njord.notes: At the blót the horn was drained to Njǫrðr and Freyr 'for good harvest and peace'; his name survives in Norwegian cult place-names such as Njarðarlǫg and Norderhov (Njarðar-hof, 'Njǫrðr's temple').

sources.reference: Snorri Sturluson, Hákonar saga góða (Heimskringla), ch. 14

norse_thor.name: libation to the idol of Thor against plague and famine at the temple of Uppsala
norse_thor.cadence: in time of dearth or plague
norse_thor.notes: Adam of Bremen describes Thor enthroned in the centre of the Uppsala temple between Wodan and Fricco, holding a scepter; when plague or famine threatened, the offering went to Thor.

sources.reference: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum, bk. 4

norse_tyr.name: offerings to Týr at his sacred groves and lakes
norse_tyr.notes: Týr's name is preserved in cult place-names such as Tislund ('Týr's grove') in Denmark; the lake Tissø ('Týr's lake') has yielded great quantities of deposited Viking-age weapons read as offerings.

sources.reference: toponymy of Tislund and Tissø; cf. de Vries, Altgermanische Religionsgeschichte

norse_ullr.name: oaths sworn upon the ring of Ullr
norse_ullr.cadence: at the swearing of solemn oaths
norse_ullr.notes: Atlakviða invokes Ullr's ring in oath-taking; his name is preserved in some thirty-odd Swedish and eastern-Norwegian cult place-names (e.g. Ullevi 'Ullr's sanctuary', Ullarlundr 'Ullr's grove'), marking an extensive early cult.

sources.reference: Atlakviða 30 (Poetic Edda); Grímnismál 42 (Ýdalir); cf. Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum bk. 3 (Ollerus)

nuer_colwic.name: the colwic shrine-rite for one taken by lightning
nuer_colwic.notes: When a person is killed by lightning the kin raise a shrine-stake (riek) on the funeral mound and plant a sapling of the nyuot tree beside it; sacrifice is made by all relatives, for the dead has been taken straight to Kwoth in the sky and become colwic.

nuer_deng.name: sacrifice of an ox to release one seized by Deng
nuer_deng.notes: An ox (or, failing that, a cucumber) is consecrated and speared so that its life may go to the spirit in place of the sufferer's, freeing the sick person from Deng.

nupe_gunnu.name: the annual Gunnu fertility festival with bush initiation of boys
nupe_gunnu.notes: Served by the hereditary Gunnuko priesthood, the dry-season festival asks renewed fertility of the land; boys undergo a rite of passage in the forest, and the Ndakó Gboyá masquerade — 'the policeman of the Gunnu' — appears.

sources.reference: S. F. Nadel, 'Gunnu, a Fertility Cult of the Nupe' (JRAI, 1937); Nadel, Nupe Religion (1954)

nupe_kuti.name: the Ndakó Gboyá masquerade performance for witch-finding and cleansing
nupe_kuti.cadence: on call and at the Gunnu festival
nupe_kuti.notes: The towering shroud-masked spirit is summoned to detect and drive out witches and to cleanse villages; performers form a secret society of priestly 'policemen' of the cult.

sources.reference: S. F. Nadel, Nupe Religion (1954); Nadel, 'Witchcraft and Anti-Witchcraft in Nupe Society' (Africa, 1935)

attributes.name: the apples of immortality she cradles
attributes.notes: Iðunn's defining attribute is the basket or casket of apples that keep the gods young.

attributes.name: the colossal serpent coiled round Midgard biting its own tail
attributes.notes: Jǫrmungandr lies in the sea encircling the world, gripping its tail in its mouth (Gylfaginning).

attributes.name: Thor's fishing of the serpent in Viking-age carving
attributes.notes: The serpent appears on Thor's fishing-line on the Altuna runestone (Uppland) and amid Ragnarök scenes on the Gosforth Cross (Cumbria).

attributes.name: the fire-giant wreathed in flame bearing a sun-bright sword
attributes.notes: Surtr comes from the south at Ragnarök with fire, his sword shining brighter than the sun, and burns the world (Vǫluspá; Gylfaginning).

sources.reference: Vǫluspá 52 (Poetic Edda); Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 4 and 51

attributes.name: the vast primordial frost-giant formed where frost met fire
attributes.notes: Ymir takes shape from the rime of Élivágar where the cold of Niflheim meets the heat of Muspell (Gylfaginning).

sacredAnimals.name: Auðhumla, the primeval cow that nourished him

attributes.name: the great thick shoe with which he braces against Fenrir's jaw
attributes.notes: Víðarr's iconic attribute is the shoe made of all the leather-scraps men cut from their shoes, by which he tears the wolf apart at Ragnarök (Gylfaginning).

sources.reference: Snorri Sturluson, Gylfaginning (Prose Edda), ch. 51; Skáldskaparmál

attributes.name: the skis, snowshoes and hunting-bow of the snow-goddess
attributes.notes: Skaði is the ǫndurdís ('snowshoe-goddess'), figured ranging the winter mountains on skis with her bow (Gylfaginning; Skáldskaparmál).

sources.reference: Snorri Sturluson, Gylfaginning and Skáldskaparmál (Prose Edda)

attributes.name: the towering cylindrical cloth figure ('the tall grandfather') that rises and shrinks
attributes.notes: Ndakó Gboyá appears as an immense column of white cloth over a hidden bearer, able to tower up and sink down, wrapped like a burial shroud.
